query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Stabilized FCC/BCC phase boundaries in the protective coating enhance creep resistance by mediating distributed dislocation transfer and limiting localized shear band formation under sustained high-temperature loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy protective coating possessing a dual-phase microstructure with an FCC matrix and embedded BCC regions formed through conventional processing, exhibiting an average (baseline) phase boundary density.
generation.intervention: A controlled heat treatment or processing modification designed to increase both the stability and density of the FCC/BCC phase boundaries without altering the overall alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Continuous mechanical loading at elevated temperatures representative of service conditions (i.e., conditions where progressive plastic deformation and creep are critical).
generation.structural_mediator: Stabilized FCC/BCC interfaces that serve as barriers to dislocation motion and facilitate dynamic load partitioning across the phases.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced phase boundary stability restricts the localized shear and promotes a cooperative dislocation-transfer or transformation mechanism (e.g., limited transformation/twinning) that distributes the strain more uniformly, thereby reducing creep deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings treated to promote higher phase boundary density will exhibit a lower creep strain rate and reduced formation of localized shear bands compared to untreated controls under identical high-temperature, sustained loading.
generation.baseline: The coating with standard processing, which presents a typical FCC/BCC phase distribution and conventional creep strain rate under service-like conditions.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to operate effectively under sustained high-temperature loading within the stress and temperature limits of the alloy; outside these limits, alternative deformation or phase transformation routes may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative role of phase boundary density versus variations in local chemical order in controlling creep resistance remains to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of high-entropy alloy protective coatings: one set using standard processing and another set with an optimized heat treatment designed to enhance FCC/BCC boundary stability. Subject both sets to identical prolonged creep tests under controlled high-temperature and sustained load conditions.
measurements: Creep strain rate measured via extensometry or digital image correlation (DIC)
Microstructural analysis using TEM/SEM to quantify phase boundary density and assess the presence of shear bands
Characterization of dislocation structures and dynamic load partitioning through high-resolution imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with enhanced phase boundary density do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate and show no appreciable differences in dislocation patterns or shear band formation relative to the control samples, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder

Abstract: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Effect of Al Content on Microstructure and Properties of AlxCr0.2NbTiV Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractHigh-temperature creep refers to the slow and continuous plastic deformation of materials under the effects of high temperatures and mechanical stress over extended periods, which can lead to the degradation or even failure of the components’ functionality. AlxCr0.2NbTiV (x = 0.2, 0.5, or 0.8) refractory high-entropy alloys were fabricated by arc melting. The effects of Al content on the microstructure of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were studied using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and electron backscatter diffraction. The microhardness, compression properties, and nanoindentation creep properties of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were also tested. The results show that the AlxCr0.2NbTiV series exhibits a BCC single-phase structure. As the Al content increases, the lattice constant of the alloys gradually decreases, and the intensity of the (110) crystal plane diffraction peak increases. Coarse slip bands and non-Schmid’s translational slip lead to shear bands formation in body-centered cubic HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe microstructural evolution and shear band formation mechanism in an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr body-centered cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloy (HEA) were systematically investigated during cold rolling. Microstructural observations revealed the development of coarse, and straight slip bands at early deformation stages. Detailed analysis of slip band–grain boundary (GB) interactions showed evidence of continuous slip transmission across GB regions. With increasing deformation, localized strain regions evolved along the prior slip bands, eventually leading to the formation of well-defined shear bands. Non-Schmid effects were found to promote slip continuity across GBs, preferentially along the {112} slip planes, thereby facilitating strain localization. Real-time observations of TRIP-induced ultrahigh strain hardening in a dual-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy

Abstract: AbstractStrategies involving metastable phases have been the basis of the design of numerous alloys, yet research on metastable high-entropy alloys is still in its infancy. In dual-phase high-entropy alloys, the combination of local chemical environments and loading-induced crystal structure changes suggests a relationship between deformation mechanisms and chemical atomic distribution, which we examine in here in a Cantor-like Cr20Mn6Fe34Co34Ni6 alloy, comprising both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal closed packed (hcp) phases. We observe that partial dislocation activities result in stable three-dimensional stacking-fault networks. Additionally, the fraction of the stronger hcp phase progressively increases during plastic deformation by forming at the stacking-fault network boundaries in the fcc phase, serving as the major source of strain hardening.
